item.title: Differentiating Eclipse Compiler (ECJ) vs Javac: Core Behavior Discrepancies
item.description:
“Differentiating Eclipse Compiler (ECJ) vs Javac: Core Behavior Discrepancies”

The Eclipse IDE employs its own sophisticated compiler, the Eclipse Compiler for Java (ECJ), which operates distinctly from the standard javac shipped with the Oracle/Sun JDK. This divergence in implementation leads to several notable operational distinctions crucial for developers using different environments.

Core Architectural Divergence: Independent Compilation Engines

The most significant revelation is that ECJ is not a wrapper around javac. It is an entirely separate compilation engine.

item.title: Generating C/C++ Assembly Code with GCC and Alternatives
item.description:
“Generating C/C++ Assembly Code with GCC and Alternatives”

Obtaining the assembly representation of high-level source code is crucial for deep performance tuning, security auditing, or simply appreciating how the compiler translates constructs. Several robust techniques exist, primarily centered around the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC) and related binutils.

Direct Assembly Generation with GCC/G++

The primary mechanism to instruct GCC or G++ to halt compilation after the assembly stage (before the assembler runs) is the -S flag.

item.title: GCC vs G++ Which C++ Compiler to Use
item.description:
“GCC vs G++ Which C++ Compiler to Use”

Delving into the world of C++ development often brings up the question: what’s the real distinction between gcc and g++? Both are integral parts of the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), yet they exhibit subtle but important differences in their default behaviors and how they handle C++ specifics. This exploration aims to clarify these distinctions, providing insights into their operational defaults and offering guidance on choosing the right tool for your C++ projects.
